title: Why Do We Need to Feel Needed?
metaTitle: Why Do We Need to Feel Needed? What the Research Shows
metaDescription: Feeling needed is a normal human drive tied to belonging and meaning. Research on mattering and generativity helps explain why it runs so deep.
keyFinding: The need to feel needed reflects a deep, well-documented human drive to matter to others and to contribute — believing you matter strongly predicts wellbeing, while feeling you don't predicts distress.
honestAnswer: Because feeling needed is one of the ways humans register that they belong and that their life has weight to other people — and that registering is closely tied to wellbeing. The drive is not a weakness or a sign of insecurity by default; it is a normal feature of a social species, and the research that comes closest to it, on what psychologists call 'mattering,' finds that believing other people depend on you and notice you is strongly linked to feeling well.

So when you feel a pull toward being useful, relied upon, or contributing something, you are responding to a deep and broadly healthy need. It can be overdone — there is a version where being needed tips into over-functioning, enmeshment, or basing your whole worth on usefulness — but the underlying need itself is normal. Understanding where it comes from tends to be more useful than trying to talk yourself out of it.
whatDataShows: Psychologists have a specific construct for this: 'mattering,' developed by Morris Rosenberg and extended by Gordon Flett and others. Mattering is the sense that you are significant to other people — that they depend on you, notice you, and would be affected by your absence. Research consistently finds that a higher sense of mattering is associated with better wellbeing and acts as a buffer against depression and loneliness.

The flip side has its own name: 'anti-mattering,' the feeling that you don't matter or are insignificant to others. Flett's work links anti-mattering to psychological distress, including symptoms of depression and a sense of disconnection. In other words, it is not just that mattering helps; the absence of it tends to actively hurt. Feeling needed is, in part, evidence to ourselves that we matter.

There is a developmental dimension too. Erik Erikson described a midlife stage organized around 'generativity' — the drive to contribute to others and to the next generation — versus 'stagnation,' a sense of self-absorption and going nowhere. In this framing, contributing to others is not a bonus but a central source of meaning in adulthood. A broader body of research on usefulness and contribution similarly links a sense of being useful to others with higher wellbeing, especially across midlife and later life.
whyItFeelsDifferent: The need to feel needed often gets quietly judged — as neediness, as ego, as not being 'secure enough' to be content alone. That framing makes the perfectly normal experience of wanting to matter feel like a flaw to fix rather than a signal to understand. The research suggests the opposite: wanting to matter is closer to a baseline human need than to a personal weakness.

It also feels different because the need usually shows up most loudly when it is going unmet — after a role ends, when children grow up, after a retirement or a loss — so people often notice the drive only as an ache. That timing can make feeling needed seem like a problem, when really the discomfort is the absence of something that was doing real work for your wellbeing.

And there is a fine line that is genuinely hard to see from the inside. Being needed can shade into over-functioning, where your worth becomes contingent on being indispensable, or into relationships organized around your usefulness rather than your presence. The need itself is healthy; it is the all-or-nothing version — 'I only matter if I'm needed' — that tends to cause trouble.
whatResearchSaysToDo: The most consistent implication of the mattering research is that the need is met by genuine, mutual connection and contribution, not by performing usefulness. Relationships where you are valued for who you are as well as what you do, and where the dependence runs both ways, tend to support a durable sense of mattering rather than a fragile, performance-based one.

Generativity research points toward contribution as a renewable source of meaning across adulthood — mentoring, caregiving, creating things others use, volunteering, or simply being reliably present for people. The form matters less than the genuine sense that what you do registers with others. This is one reason transitions that strip away a contributing role, like retirement, can hit wellbeing, and why finding new avenues to contribute tends to help.

It also helps to broaden the base of mattering beyond a single role. When the entire sense of mattering rests on one relationship or one job, its loss can be destabilizing. Research on wellbeing across life transitions generally favors having several sources of connection and contribution, so that mattering does not stand or fall on one thing.
whatDoesNotHelp: Trying to suppress the need or shame yourself out of it does not tend to help, and can make things worse. Treating a normal human drive as a defect usually adds self-criticism on top of an unmet need, rather than resolving it. The research frames mattering as something to meet, not to eliminate.

Making yourself indispensable as a strategy is a common trap that tends to backfire. Over-functioning — taking on more and more so others depend on you — can produce burnout, resentment, and relationships that feel transactional, and it leaves you fragile when the need for you changes. Being needed for everything is not the same as mattering to someone.

Buying status or chasing achievement to feel significant is a poor substitute for genuine mattering. The evidence on relative status and acquisition suggests these are subject to comparison and adaptation, so the sense of significance they buy tends to be brief. Mattering appears to come from being noticed and depended on by specific people, not from impressing a general audience.
realNumbersInContext: There is no single clean statistic that captures 'the need to feel needed,' and inventing one would be dishonest. What the research offers instead is a consistent pattern: across studies, a higher sense of mattering is associated with better mental health and a lower risk of depression and loneliness, while anti-mattering — feeling insignificant to others — is associated with greater distress. The direction is steady even though exact effect sizes vary by study and population.

The broader context is that this need sits alongside some of the most robust findings in wellbeing research: that close relationships and a sense of contribution are among the strongest correlates of a meaningful, satisfying life. Feeling needed is one of the channels through which those larger forces operate — which is why the drive is so common and why its absence is felt so sharply.

faqs.question: Is it unhealthy to need to feel needed?
faqs.answer: Not in itself. Wanting to matter to others and to contribute is a normal, well-documented human drive tied to belonging and meaning. It becomes a problem mainly in its extreme form — when your entire sense of worth depends on being indispensable, which can tip into over-functioning and burnout. The need is healthy; the all-or-nothing version is what tends to cause trouble.

faqs.question: What is 'mattering' in psychology?
faqs.answer: Mattering is the sense that you are significant to other people — that they depend on you, notice you, and would be affected by your absence. The concept comes from Morris Rosenberg and was extended by Gordon Flett. A higher sense of mattering is consistently linked to better wellbeing and lower risk of depression and loneliness.

faqs.question: Why does feeling useless feel so bad?
faqs.answer: Research on 'anti-mattering' — the feeling that you don't matter to others — links it to psychological distress, including depressive symptoms and disconnection. Feeling needed is partly how we confirm to ourselves that we matter, so its absence registers not as neutral but as actively painful.

faqs.question: Why does this hit harder after kids leave or after retirement?
faqs.answer: Those transitions remove a major role through which people contributed and felt depended upon. Erikson's idea of 'generativity' frames contributing to others as central to meaning in adulthood, so losing a contributing role can leave a real gap. Finding new avenues to contribute and connect tends to help fill it.

faqs.question: How can I meet this need in a healthy way?
faqs.answer: The research points toward genuine, mutual relationships where you're valued for who you are and not just what you do, and toward real contribution in whatever form fits — mentoring, caregiving, creating, volunteering. It also helps to spread the sources of mattering across several relationships and roles, so it doesn't all rest on one.

Flett, G. L. — research on mattering and 'anti-mattering' and their links to wellbeing, depression, and loneliness.
Erikson, E. H. — psychosocial development and the midlife stage of generativity versus stagnation.
